extracted.intended_audience: activity comptrollers, contracting officers, procurement/acquisition staff (DoD/federal agencies)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for DoD/Federal contracting and implementation of OMB Circular A-76 commercial activity studies, including methods of contracting, contract types, the A-76 cost-comparison process (MEO/PWS), and decision thresholds for converting services to commercial sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procurement Contracting Officer (PCO) responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: This individual is responsible for the overall contract; specifically, activities leading up to and awarding of the contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCO leads the solicitation and award phases and is the primary contracting official for the procurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Contracting Officer (ACO) role
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual monitors contractor performance after the contract award and acts as the Government's 'eyes and ears' in the contractor’s plant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACO performs post-award surveillance, ensures contract compliance, and reports to the PCO and program manager.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination Contracting Officer (TCO) responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsible for all actions leading to settlements of terminated contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TCO handles contract termination actions and settlement procedures when contracts are ended prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense Contract Audit Agency (DCAA) function
rubrics_metrics.description: DCAA audits contractors’ books and accounting records regarding the acceptability and allowability of estimated and incurred costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use DCAA audits to validate cost proposals and in-house cost estimates where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of contracting — sealed bidding vs competitive negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two major methods: sealed bid (competitive bids, public opening, awards) and competitive negotiation (use of proposals and discussions); both placed on equal basis by Competition in Contracting Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select sealed bidding only when its specific criteria are satisfied; otherwise use negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sealed bidding permissibility criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Sealed bidding is permitted if: (1) Time permits solicitation, submission and evaluation of sealed bids; (2) Award can be made on price or other price-related factors; (3) Conducting discussions with bidders is not necessary; (4) There is a reasonable expectation of receiving more than one sealed bid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any of these conditions are not met, sealed bidding should not be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sealed bidding contract types and process steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Sealed bidding uses an Invitation for Bid (IFB) and must use either a Firm Fixed Price (FFP) contract or a Fixed Price with Economic Price Adjustment contract. Steps: prepare IFB (clear, concise, complete description), publicize IFB, receive submission by deadline, evaluate bids without discussions, award based on price/price-related factors to most advantageous bidder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure IFB description is flawless; evaluate bids without engaging bidders in discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of negotiation method
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiation (competitive or other-than-competitive proposals and discussions) is used whenever sealed bid criteria cannot be met; characterized by bargaining and revision of offers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiations generally cover price, schedule, contract type and terms; multiple contractors do not usually negotiate simultaneously for same contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost/pricing data requirement in negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractors are required to submit cost and pricing data used by Contracting Officers in negotiating prices and other terms when the cost of the contract exceeds $500,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and analyze certified cost/pricing data for negotiations above threshold to establish fair and reasonable prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory exceptions allowing sole source contracting
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Competition in Contracting Act there are seven statutory exceptions permitting sole source contracting: (1) Only one responsible source; (2) Unusual or compelling urgency; (3) Industrial mobilization purposes; (4) Based on an international agreement or Foreign Military Sales requirement; (5) To meet a statutory requirement; (6) In the interest of national security; (7) In the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sole source contracts must be formally justified and receive appropriate approval level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special contracting methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Special methods include multi-year contracting, options, and leader company contracting; each has specific limitations, objectives and requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use special methods to increase economic efficiency where appropriate; evaluate objectives and constraints for each method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider when selecting contract type
rubrics_metrics.description: Key factors include: (1) Price competition, (2) Cost analysis, (3) Price analysis, (4) Urgency of requirement, (5) Type and complexity of requirement, (6) Adequacy of contractor’s accounting system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess these factors and negotiate a contract type that allocates risk and incentives appropriately between government and contractor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract type categories — fixed-price vs cost-reimbursement
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract types vary by degree/timing of contractor cost responsibility and profit incentive; generally divided into Fixed-Price contracts and Cost-Reimbursement contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose fixed-price when risk can be reasonably allocated to contractor; choose cost-reimbursement when high uncertainty/risk precludes fixed price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm Fixed Price (FFP) contract features
rubrics_metrics.description: Government and contractor agree to a fixed price not subject to adjustment; places maximum risk on contractor who assumes full responsibility for cost control and any loss or profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FFP provides maximum incentive for contractor to control costs; use when requirements and prices are stable and well-defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-Price Redeterminable contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Used when uncertainties preclude use of FFP; provides a firm fixed price for an initial period and prospective redetermination at specified times for subsequent periods; contractor must have acceptable cost accounting for redetermination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suitable where long-term uncertainties exist but contractor accounting can support future price redeterminations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-Price Incentive contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractor and Government agree on target costs and a pricing agreement with an incentive share formula; contractor shares savings if under target and suffers reduced profit for overruns; a price ceiling is negotiated; divided into firm target or successive targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to incentivize cost reduction while allowing adjustment via share/ceiling mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Plus-Incentive Fee contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifies a target cost, target profit, minimum and maximum fees and a fee adjustment formula; fee is adjusted based on relationship between allowable costs and target costs; typically used for high-risk projects without a price ceiling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages contractor cost control on high-risk efforts where fixed-price is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Plus-Award Fee contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides a fixed base fee plus an award amount based on excellence in quality, timeliness, technical ingenuity, and cost-effective management; Government can realign weights in award fee formula each award period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to reward superior performance and permit flexibility in weighting performance attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides contractor reimbursement for allowable costs plus a fixed fee; usually used where great risks and uncertainties exist (e.g., R&D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed fee remains constant regardless of actual costs; appropriate for uncertain work where incentives via variable fees are not feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other contract/agreements and their uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Other vehicles: indefinite quantity contracts, definite quantity contracts, requirements contracts, time-and-materials contracts, labor-hour contracts, letter contracts, basic ordering agreements, and purchase agreements; each suited to particular procurement needs (e.g., unknown quantities, small purchases, repetitive procurement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the vehicle matching the procurement's quantity certainty, delivery timing, and administrative needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracting process phases and key activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Process phases: (1) Planning — determine procurement method, acquisition strategy, contract type, develop solicitation and data for negotiation; (2) Solicitation release/clarification — issue solicitation, modifications, bidder conferences; (3) Source evaluation & selection — evaluate bids/offers, determine lowest responsive/responsible bidder/offeror, establish competitive range, apply source selection criteria, prepare for negotiations using cost/price analysis; (4) Negotiation — negotiate schedule, costs, pricing structure, profit/fee, technical aspects (not applicable to sealed bids); (5) Award — final agreement, contract preparation, legal review, signatures, publicizing award; (6) Contract administration — monitor performance, production surveillance, quality assurance, cost auditing, termination settlements, property management, payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow each phase methodically; ensure documentation and compliance at each step to support award decisions and post-award administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular A-76 core principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Three principles: (1) Achieve economy and enhance productivity by comparing contracting vs in-house performance; (2) Retain inherently governmental functions in-house; (3) Rely on the commercial sector for commercially available products/services and avoid starting commercial activities in government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these principles to determine whether to contract out functions and to structure cost comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: A-76 study components — SOW/PWS, Quality Assurance Plan, MEO, and cost baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: A commercial activity study begins with task analysis to produce a Statement of Work (SOW) that becomes a Performance Work Statement (PWS); concurrently design a Quality Assurance plan; develop a Most Efficient Organization (MEO) and prepare in-house cost estimate as baseline for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PWS accuracy and scope are critical; MEO must reflect a streamlined organization; QA plan ensures government can monitor contractor performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation requirements for A-76 competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicitation must notify contractors that award is based solely on a cost comparison between commercial bidders and the government's MEO estimate, and must inform contractors they are required to offer employment to any qualified government employee displaced as a result of the commercial activity study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly include these stipulations in solicitation documents to ensure bidders understand award basis and employee placement obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: A-76 winning threshold and bid coverage durations
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon receipt of bids, the lower of contractor bid or MEO cost is selected; contractor proposals must be at least ten percent less than the MEO to be judged a winner. For multi-year funding bids will be for a minimum of three years; for single-year funding bids will cover two fiscal years after the initial year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 10% threshold and multi-year coverage rules when comparing bids to the MEO baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of review for in-house retained commercial activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial activities retained in-house must be reviewed again five years after the original study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a schedule for periodic reviews to reassess conversion potential and cost-effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Returning a contracted activity to in-house performance standard
rubrics_metrics.description: To convert a contracted commercial activity back to in-house performance, the new MEO must demonstrate performing the activity in-house would be ten percent cheaper than the cost charged by the commercial source plus 25 percent of the commercial source’s capital assets cost (resulting in at least a 20 percent improvement over original MEO in many cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the high cost-savings threshold and approval authority (Secretary/Director) required to return activities in-house.

rubrics_metrics.name: A-76 implementation process phases
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation considers existing activities, expansion of activities, and new requirements; the conversion process consists of four phases: inventory, management review, cost comparison, and implementation of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor steps within each phase depending on whether the service is existing or a new requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventory and FTE threshold for existing services
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventory separates activities into those with 10 or fewer full-time equivalent (FTE) work years and those with more than 10 FTEs; one FTE roughly equals one employee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities with less than 10 FTEs should be considered for conversion if costs are reasonable; use FTE grouping to prioritize reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management review decision criteria (existing services)
rubrics_metrics.description: Management review asks: Is activity a governmental function? Is in-house performance required for national defense? Is in-house performance required at a government hospital by agency medical director? Are satisfactory commercial sources available? Would unacceptable delay occur? Will contract be awarded under a Preferential Procurement Program (PPP)? Are less than ten FTEs present? Does Assistant Secretary waive cost comparison? Will contract cost be unreasonable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If activity is governmental or any review condition precludes contracting out, retain in-house and stop the review; otherwise proceed to cost comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost comparison outcome criteria (existing services)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after cost comparison (using Performance Work Statement and MEO), contract costs are less than in-house costs by the specified margin (typically 10% for personnel and specified rules for equipment), the contract may be awarded to the commercial sector; otherwise continue government performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure PWS and MEO cost estimate are accurate and defensible; the 10% personnel margin is a central decision threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision criteria for new services
rubrics_metrics.description: For new requirements the eight-step process includes the same initial checks (governmental function, national defense, agency medical need, availability of satisfactory commercial source, PPP award, reasonableness of contract costs). If a cost comparison is conducted, a contract is awarded if total contract costs are less than total in-house estimates by 10% of personnel costs and less than 25% of acquisition costs for equipment and plant necessary to perform the service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the 10% (personnel) and 25% (equipment/plant) margins when evaluating new service procurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of accurate PWS and capture of outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Task analysis for developing the PWS must identify and quantify the output generated by the activity; the PWS is the basis of both the Government’s and commercial sources’ cost estimates and solicitation documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PWS accuracy and flawless scope are essential to obtain true and comparable cost estimates; poor PWS leads to unreliable cost comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of comptroller in A-76
rubrics_metrics.description: The activity comptroller must be aware of the contracting process, methods, types of contracts and applicable laws/regulations; primary mission is efficient and economical use of government funds, monitoring requisitioning, acquisition and contracting and seeking ways to decrease costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comptroller involvement ranges from funding oversight to full administration of A-76 studies; provide technical guidance on financial matters and ensure fiscal compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and staffing expectations for A-76 administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Personnel administering A-76 need training, particularly in preparation of the Statement of Work and familiarity with the functions being studied; turnover among program analysts can undermine continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in qualified personnel, training, and retention to ensure high-quality management studies and accurate cost data capture.
